LLM · 02 · Attention and transformers

From vectors to language: attention, transformers and GPT

The previous deck ended with a (B, T, d) tensor in which every row knows its token and its position, and nothing else. This deck is the journey from that tensor to a model that predicts the next token: a mechanism that lets rows read each other, a block that makes the reading trainable at depth, and a stack of blocks with a head on top.

Enter or Space: next step · Shift+Enter: back · ← →: skip whole slides · N: study notes · click the page number for the slide list · sliders, buttons and hover readouts are live

How to use this deck

  • Press Enter to reveal the next piece of a slide; the dots at the bottom centre count the steps. The notes panel (N) gives every slide from three angles: Visually (what the picture is), Mathematically (the formula), Numerically (the real numbers, computed by the code in src/core/), then where it lives in your code and a question to check yourself.
  • Every matrix shown is the output of your own modules in a fresh process: ids [2, 1, 3] ("cat ate the") through EmbeddingLayer(6, 4, 8, 'learned'), then MultiHeadAttention(4, 2), TransformerBlock(4, 2) and GPT(6, 4, 2, 2, 8), all with the module-level default_rng(7). The last section adds a real training run of a 7,104-parameter GPT on a 107-word text.

The story in one paragraph

A row of X knows its token and its position but not its neighbours, so a context-dependent prediction is impossible from one row alone. Self-attention fixes this: each row asks a question (query), every row advertises what it holds (key) and what it would hand over (value); dot products score the matches, a softmax turns scores into weights, and each row becomes a weighted average of the values. Dividing by √d keeps the softmax from saturating; a causal mask keeps a position from reading the future. One softmax row can express only one pattern, so the dimension is split into heads that attend independently and are concatenated. Attention only mixes rows linearly, so a block wraps it with LayerNorm, a per-position MLP and residual connections, which makes a deep stack trainable. GPT is an embedding, N such blocks under a causal mask, a final norm and a linear head to the vocabulary; its goal is next-token prediction at every position at once, trained with the cross-entropy, autograd and optimizer from the foundation decks.

01 · Recap · Tokenization

Recap 1: a tokenizer turns text into integer IDs

A network only adds and multiplies, so text is cut into units from a fixed vocabulary of size V and each unit gets an integer. The only decision is how big a unit is.

A word tokenizer: a sorted set and two dictionaries

Corpus "cat ate the tuna" + "wolf ate the cat" → vocabulary ['<UNK>', 'ate', 'cat', 'the', 'tuna', 'wolf'], V = 6. The CharTokenizer recipe (sorted set, <UNK> first, two dictionaries) applied to words, so the examples read naturally. Nothing is learned.

BPETokenizer: grow the vocabulary by merging

Start from characters, count adjacent pairs, merge the most frequent pair into one token, repeat until V is reached. Common fragments become single tokens; any string can still be spelled.

What this deck inherits: ids of shape (B, T)

V sets the embedding table (V × d) and the size of the output head; T sets the cost of attention, which will be T² per head per layer. The running example of this deck: "cat ate the" → [2, 1, 3].

src/core/tokenization.py · CharTokenizer.build_vocab sorts the character set and puts <UNK> first; this deck applies the same recipe to whitespace-split words. BPETokenizer.train repeats _count_byte_pairs and _merge_pair; merges shown are its first two on the word list. Full treatment: deck 01, sections 01–03.

Visually

  • Step 1: the corpus, the sorted word set, and the vocabulary table with its ids. Encoding "cat ate the" walks the table: cat → 2, ate → 1, the → 3.
  • Step 2: BPE in one picture, run by your BPETokenizer on the words of the corpus: it starts from characters (11 of them, plus <UNK>), the pair (c, a) occurs twice, so "ca" becomes a token; then (ca, t) gives "cat" as a single token. Several pairs tie at 2; Counter.most_common takes the first seen. Each merge shortens the spelling of the corpus by one token per occurrence.
  • Step 3: the output of the tokenizer is what everything downstream sees: a (B, T) array of integers.

Mathematically

A tokenizer is a bijection between strings over its vocabulary and sequences of ids. The ids are names, not quantities: 3 is not "three times 1", which is why the next step replaces each id with a vector. BPE training greedily minimises the number of tokens needed to write the training corpus, one merge at a time.

Numerically

"cat ate the" → [2, 1, 3]; decode([2, 1, 3]) → "cat ate the". A word missing from the vocabulary maps to 0 (<UNK>), so encode("cat ate fish") → [2, 1, 0] and decoding gives "cat ate <UNK>": the only lossy case.

In your code

CharTokenizer and BPETokenizer in src/core/tokenization.py; create_tokenizer(strategy, vocab_size, corpus) builds either. The repo has no word tokenizer: this deck's word vocabulary is ['<UNK>'] + sorted(set(text.split())), the CharTokenizer recipe on words. The tiny GPT trained at the end of this deck uses it with V = 12.

Check yourself

  • Why does the choice of tokenizer change the cost of attention? It fixes T for a given text; attention does T² work per head per layer.

01 · Recap · Embedding

Recap 2: an embedding turns each ID into a learned vector

A one-hot vector times a (V × d) table is a row of the table, so the lookup is a gather: E = W[ids]. Backward, the gradient is scattered back into the rows that were picked.

Gather forward, scatter-add backward

∂L/∂W is zero except in rows 2, 1 and 3, which receive the three gradient rows of E. A repeated id accumulates; rows never picked are untouched this step.

Similarity becomes geometry

Two ids whose rows point the same way will be treated alike by every layer above. At init the rows are random; the loss moves them. Attention is built on exactly this: dot products between learned vectors.

Numbers: Embedding(6, 4).weight drawn with numpy default_rng(7) as in src/core/embeddings.py (uniform ±√(6/(V+d)) = ±0.775). The same W as deck 01.

Visually

  • Step 1: ids [2, 1, 3] pick rows 2, 1, 3 of W. Row colours follow the id, as in deck 01, so you can trace each token through the deck.
  • Step 2: backward reverses the arrows: each gradient row of E is added into the row of W it came from.
  • Step 3: what the table is for. Everything the model knows about a token, before it sees its neighbours, is in its row.

Mathematically

E = onehot(ids) · W, with onehot of shape (T, V) and W of shape (V, d); indexing skips the zeros. ∂L/∂W = onehot(ids)ᵀ · ∂L/∂E, which is the scatter-add.

Numerically

W[2] = [0.460, −0.050, −0.305, −0.343] is the row for "cat"; W[1] = [−0.310, 0.579, −0.766, 0.498] for "ate"; W[3] = [−0.380, −0.085, 0.007, 0.083] for "the". E is these three rows stacked, shape (3, 4). 24 parameters here; GPT-2's table is 50,257 × 768 = 38.6M.

In your code

Embedding.forward does self.weight.data[indices] and attaches EmbeddingBackward(weight, indices), whose apply uses np.add.at. Note the typo self.indices.dota in that method: backward raises until it reads .data (the recap slide lists every fix needed to train end to end).

Check yourself

  • If the batch contains "cat ate the tuna" and "wolf ate the cat", how many rows of ∂L/∂W are nonzero? Five: ate, cat, the, tuna, wolf. Row 0 (<UNK>) is never picked.

01 · Recap · Position, and the gap

Recap 3: positions are added, and each row is still blind to its neighbours

X = E + P[:T] stamps where each token sits. But X[t] depends only on the token at t and on t itself: swap every other token in the sentence and the row does not change.

The gap

The "the" row of "cat ate the" and of "wolf ate the" is the same vector, number for number. A row-wise layer, a Linear or an MLP, gives the same output for both: the next word cannot be told apart.

Why only the last row is framed

The "ate" rows are identical too (W[1] + P[1] in both). The last row is framed because, under the causal mask, its output is the next-word prediction: identical last rows force the same guess after a cat and after a wolf.

What is needed

A layer whose output row t is a function of all rows, where the dependence is decided by the content of the rows, and which works for any T. That layer is self-attention, section 03.

Numbers: PositionalEncoding(8, 4) rows 0…2, default_rng(7) after the token table, as in deck 01. X[2] for "cat ate the" and "wolf ate the" is W[3] + P[2] in both cases; X[1] is W[1] + P[1] in both.

Visually

  • Step 1: E (3 × 4) plus the first three rows of the position table P (8 × 4) gives X. The grey rows of P are unused for T = 3.
  • Step 2: a second sentence, "wolf ate the": ids [5, 1, 3]. Its first row differs (W[5] instead of W[2]) but its second and third rows are identical to those of "cat ate the". The frame sits on the third row because that is the row whose output predicts the next word.
  • Steps 3–4: the gap and the requirement. This is the whole motivation of the deck in one picture.

Mathematically

X[t] = W[idt] + P[t]. The right-hand side has no term that involves ids for s ≠ t. A row-wise map f gives f(X)[t] = f(X[t]), so f(Xcat ate the)[2] = f(Xwolf ate the)[2] for every f.

Numerically

X[2] = W[3] + P[2] = [−0.380, −0.085, 0.007, 0.083] + [−0.690, −0.435, 0.272, −0.423] = [−1.070, −0.520, 0.279, −0.340], in both sentences. X[0] for "cat ate the" is [−0.196, −0.029, −0.353, 0.247]; for "wolf ate the" it is W[5] + P[0] = [−1.098, −0.505, 0.127, −0.117].

In your code

EmbeddingLayer.forward: gather, optional × √d, then PositionalEncoding.forward adds position_embeddings[:seq_len] with a broadcast batch axis. GPT.__init__ creates exactly this layer first. One bug to know: the batch axis is added by wrapping .data[np.newaxis] in a fresh Tensor, which detaches P from the graph, so in the training run of section 06 the position table never moved; the recap slide lists the fix.

Check yourself

  • Would sinusoidal positions close the gap? No: they also depend only on t, not on the other tokens.

02 · Why attention

The challenge: rows must read each other, selectively

Two options that fall short

A · sum or average the rows: one vector for the whole sentence, the same for every position and every order; blind to who is where. B · a recurrent state: position t sees a summary of 0…t−1, but the T steps run one after another and a signal from 12 tokens back has crossed 12 multiplications.

Option C: let each row choose its sources

Row t forms its own weighted average of all rows, with weights computed from the rows' contents: every position in parallel, one hop to any distance, weights learned. This is self-attention.

Proof that it is needed, from your own code

The tiny GPT of section 06 reads "the bone . the cat sat on the" and predicts mat (0.99); "the fish . the dog sat on the" and predicts log (1.00). The last rows are identical; only the word 3 positions back differs. No row-wise layer could do this.

Arcs on the sentence are illustrative weights. The bar charts are real: probe outputs of GPT(V=12, d=16, 2 layers, 2 heads, T=8) after 401 Adam steps, src/core/transformers.py through your autograd. The sentence before each probe is deliberately from the other animal, so it cannot be used as a shortcut.

Visually

  • Step 1: "the cat sat on the mat because it was tired". To predict what follows "it was", the model must know that "it" is the cat. The arcs show what we want: the row for "it" draws mostly from "cat", a little from "tired" and "sat", almost nothing from "the".
  • Steps 2–3: the three ways to let rows interact, and why the third wins: content-based, parallel, any distance.
  • Step 4: the same requirement with real numbers. The last position of "the bone . the cat sat on the" must find "cat" to choose "mat" over "log". Your trained model does: mat 0.994 against log 0.003; for the dog probe log 0.996 against mat 0.002.

Mathematically

Wanted: outputi = Σj aij · (something from row j), with aij ≥ 0, Σj aij = 1, and aij a function of X[i] and X[j]. Option A is aij = 1/T for all i, j. Option B has no such closed form: the state is a product of T Jacobians. Option C is attention: aij = softmaxj(score(X[i], X[j])).

Numerically

Before training, the same model gave the cat probe "log" at 0.42 and the dog probe "log" at 0.41: the same guess for both, exactly the blindness of the recap. After 401 steps the right answer carries 0.99. Section 06 opens the attention weights of this model and shows which earlier words the last row reads.

In your code

Nothing yet: this slide is the specification that scaled_dot_product_attention in src/core/attention.py fulfils.

Check yourself

  • Option A is a special case of option C. What are its weights? aij = 1/T: uniform attention, which is also what attention looks like at initialisation (section 03).

03 · Self-attention · Q, K, V

Three projections of the same X: what I look for, what I offer, what I hand over

Each row is sent through three Linear layers. Q is the question a row asks, K is the label a row shows to the others, V is the content it gives away if chosen. "Self" because all three come from the same X.

One row of Q, by hand

Q[0] = X[0] · Wq
Q[0][0] = −0.196·0.0006 + (−0.029)(−0.227)
  + (−0.353)(−0.246) + 0.247·0.053
  = −0.0001 + 0.0065 + 0.0869 + 0.0130 = 0.1062

Why three matrices and not one

The question a token asks and the label it shows are different things: "it" asks for a noun; "cat" shows "I am a noun" and hands over "animal, singular". With one shared projection a token could only match tokens like itself.

All the learning is here

Wq, Wk, Wv are the only parameters before the output projection: 3(d² + d) = 60 numbers for d = 4. Everything after them, scores, softmax, averaging, is parameter-free arithmetic.

Numbers: MultiHeadAttention(4, 2).q_proj / k_proj / v_proj, the first three Linear(4, 4) drawn from layers.rng = default_rng(7), scale √(1/4) = 0.5; biases start at zero. X is the "cat ate the" tensor from the recap.

Visually

  • Step 1: X, three rows (cat, ate, the) of four numbers. Step 2: X · Wq gives Q, three rows of four: each token's question. Step 3: X · Wk gives K, each token's label. Step 4: X · Wv gives V, each token's deliverable.
  • The three weight matrices have the same shape (d × d) and the same input. Nothing forces them apart except the gradient: at init they are three independent random draws.
  • Step 5: where the parameters are. The arrows to the right (scores, softmax, mixing) have none.

Mathematically

Q = X Wq + bq, K = X Wk + bk, V = X Wv + bv, each (T, d) → (T, d). In this deck dmodel = dk = dv = 4 for the single-head picture; with heads, each head sees d/h columns (section 04). Biases are zero at init, so Q = X Wq exactly here.

Numerically

X[0] = [−0.1964, −0.0286, −0.3529, 0.2467]. Wq column 0 = [0.0006, −0.2273, −0.2461, 0.0527]. The dot product is 0.1062, which is Q[0][0] in the figure. Q[0] = [0.106, −0.020, −0.064, 0.091]; K[2] = [1.228, 0.261, 1.257, 0.626] is the largest key because X[2] has the largest norm (1.27) and Wk happens to have the largest entries.

In your code

MultiHeadAttention.__init__ builds q_proj, k_proj, v_proj, out_proj as Linear(embed_dim, embed_dim); forward step 2 applies the first three to the same x. Linear.forward is x.matmul(W) + b, which for a 3-D x goes to np.matmul.

Check yourself

  • Cross-attention in an encoder–decoder uses the same code with one change. Which? Q comes from one sequence, K and V from another.

03 · Self-attention · Scores

Scores: every question against every label, one dot product each

S = Q Kᵀ is a (T × T) table. S[i][j] is the dot product of token i's query with token j's key, an unnormalised correlation of row i of Q with row j of K: the bigger, the better j's label matches what i is looking for.

Dot product = similarity

qi · kj = ‖qi‖‖kj‖ cos θ: large when the two vectors point the same way and are long, negative when they point apart. Training shapes Wq and Wk so that a question and its matching label come out similar.

Read the table two ways

Across row i: how well each key matches token i's question. Down column j: how well token j's key matches every question. S[i][i] is a token against itself, nothing special: row 2 ("the") scores highest on itself (0.376) only because k2 is the longest key.

T² entries

Three tokens give 9 scores; 1,024 tokens give 1,048,576, per head, per layer. This is the price of letting every row look at every row, and the reason context length is expensive.

_compute_attention_scores(Q, K) = Q.matmul(K.transpose(-2, -1)) in src/core/attention.py. S[0][2] = q₀ · k₂ = 0.1305 − 0.0053 − 0.0804 + 0.0570 = 0.1018.

Visually

  • Step 1: Q (3 × 4) on the left, Kᵀ (4 × 3) on top: K with rows turned into columns. Step 2: the product S (3 × 3): cell (i, j) is row i of Q against column j of Kᵀ, i.e. qi · kj, the similarity between token i's query and token j's key. Step 3: the highlighted cell S[0][2] with its four products written out.
  • Hover any cell of S: the matching row of Q and column of Kᵀ light up and the four products are printed. Each cell costs d multiplications; the table costs T² d.

Mathematically

S = Q Kᵀ, (T × d)(d × T) → (T × T). Sij = Σm Qim Kjm, the same arithmetic as a correlation without the normalisation by the norms. The transpose makes "row of Q times row of K" into an ordinary matrix product, so one matmul does all T² dot products at once; in NumPy, np.matmul over the batch dimensions.

Numerically

S = [[−0.004, −0.065, 0.102], [−0.019, −0.007, 0.073], [0.124, 0.133, 0.376]]. All entries are small because X has norm ≈ 1 and the projections scale by 0.5: the dot products of two vectors of norm ≈ 0.2–1.4 in 4 dimensions. Column 2 is the largest everywhere: every token "likes" the "the" label most, for now.

In your code

_compute_attention_scores: K_t = K.transpose(-2, -1); return Q.matmul(K_t). Tensor.transpose with no arguments swaps the last two axes, which keeps batch and head axes in place: (B, h, T, dh) → (B, h, dh, T).

Check yourself

  • Shape of S for a batch of 8 sequences, 12 heads, T = 1024? (8, 12, 1024, 1024): 100M numbers, 400 MB in float32, per layer, before softmax.

03 · Self-attention · Scaling

Divide by √dk, or the softmax saturates at once

Random d-vectors with unit-variance entries have dot products of std √d. At d = 64 that is 8: scores of ±15 are routine, and their softmax is a one-hot with a dead gradient. Dividing by √d brings the spread back to 1.

Std of a dot product, step by step

A single dot product is one number; over many random (q, k) pairs those numbers spread out. Each product qmkm has mean 0 and variance 1·1 = 1, and the d independent products add their variances: Var(q · k) = d, std = √d. At d = 64 a typical score is ±8; ±15 is two standard deviations, routine in a long row.

Why ±15 is one-hot, and why ÷√d fixes it

Softmax only sees differences: a gap of 15 between the top two scores is a ratio e¹⁵ ≈ 3.3 million, so the winner takes all and the rest print as 0.000. Dividing by √d gives variance d/d = 1 for any d: the row lives within about ±3, exponentials differ by tens, not millions, and the softmax keeps a gradient.

Two words in the lede

Unit variance: each entry of q and k is a random number with variance 1, so of typical size 1, what initialisation and LayerNorm aim for. d: the length of one query or key vector, dk: the embedding size for a single head (64 → divisor 8), head_dim with heads (GPT-2: 768 / 12 = 64).

Measured on 20,000 random pairs

std(q · k) = 2.00, 4.01, 7.96, 15.94 for d = 4, 16, 64, 256; √d = 2, 4, 8, 16. Each product qmkm has variance 1 and the d of them add.

One query against 8 keys, d = 64

Raw scores range from −6.8 to 14.4: softmax gives 0.571 and 0.429 to two keys and exactly 0.000 to the other six. Divided by 8 the same row spreads: 0.36, 0.35, 0.09, 0.08, …

Why a dead softmax cannot learn

∂softmaxi/∂sj = pi(δij − pj). When one p is 1 and the rest 0, every entry is 0: no gradient reaches the scores, so none reaches Wq and Wk, and the pattern is frozen, not just poor. Over 5,000 random rows the largest weight averages 0.875 unscaled and 0.361 scaled.

_scale_scores(scores, d) multiplies by 1/√d in src/core/attention.py, called with Q.shape[-1] = head_dim. Std curve: default_rng(7), 20,000 pairs per d.

Visually

  • Step 1: measured standard deviation of q · k against d, with the √d curve through it. The growth is the problem: the bigger the model, the more extreme the raw scores.
  • Step 2: a real row of eight raw scores (d = 64) as bars, and the softmax of it. Drag the slider to divide by 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16 and watch the softmax go from one-hot to spread to nearly flat. √64 = 8 is the designed value.
  • Step 3: the reason saturation is fatal, not just unhelpful: the softmax Jacobian is zero at a one-hot.

Mathematically

If qm, km are independent with mean 0 and variance 1, then Var(q · k) = Σ Var(qmkm) = d, so std = √d. With 1,024 keys in a row the largest raw score is typically about 3σ, around 25 for d = 64. Scaled scores S/√dk have unit variance regardless of d. The softmax of a vector with entries spread over ±3 is already close to one-hot; ±1 keeps it soft.

Numerically

Raw row: [−2.84, 14.45, −5.96, 14.16, 2.89, −5.03, −6.75, 3.19] → softmax [0, 0.571, 0, 0.429, 0, 0, 0, 0]. Divided by 8: [−0.35, 1.81, −0.75, 1.77, 0.36, −0.63, −0.84, 0.40] → [0.041, 0.358, 0.028, 0.345, 0.084, 0.031, 0.025, 0.088]. For the "cat ate the" example d = 4, so the divisor is 2: S[2][2] = 0.376 becomes 0.188.

In your code

scaled_dot_product_attention calls _scale_scores(scores, Q.shape[-1]). Because MultiHeadAttention splits heads before calling it, Q.shape[-1] is head_dim, exactly as the formula wants (√dk, not √dmodel). Scaling is a Tensor * float, so autograd records a MulBackward.

Check yourself

  • GPT-2 small: dmodel = 768, 12 heads. What is the divisor? √64 = 8, not √768 ≈ 27.7.

03 · Self-attention · Softmax

Softmax turns each row of scores into weights that sum to one

Exponentiate so everything is positive and larger scores dominate, then divide by the row sum so the row is a distribution. Row i is "how token i splits its attention".

Row 2, by hand

exp(0.0618) = 1.0637   exp(0.0667) = 1.0690
exp(0.1882) = 1.2070   sum = 3.3397
A[2] = [0.3185, 0.3201, 0.3614]

At init, attention is almost uniform

Every row here is within 0.03 of 1/3. Random projections give small, similar scores, so the layer starts as option A (averaging). Training is what makes rows peaky: the trained model in section 06 has rows with a 0.91 entry.

Softmax is per row, over the key axis

Softmax()(scores, dim=−1): the last axis is the key position j. Columns do not sum to one; a popular source can receive more than 1 in total.

Softmax.forward in src/core/activations.py subtracts the row max before exp for stability; autograd replaces it with a tracked version that attaches SoftmaxBackward. Values: scaled scores of the "cat ate the" example, divisor √4 = 2.

Visually

  • Step 1: the scaled scores S/2. Step 2: exp of every entry: all positive, between 0.97 and 1.21 here. Step 3: each row divided by its sum gives A, and the bars on the right show that every row sums to 1.
  • Step 4: the two observations: nearly uniform at init; normalised along rows only.

Mathematically

Aij = exp(Sij/√d) / Σj' exp(Sij'/√d). Subtracting the row maximum before exponentiating changes nothing (the factor cancels) but prevents overflow. Backward, within row i: ∂Aij/∂Sik = Aij(δjk − Aik)/√d, which the code applies as A ⊙ (g − Σ(g ⊙ A)).

Numerically

A = [[0.331, 0.321, 0.349], [0.328, 0.330, 0.343], [0.319, 0.320, 0.361]]. Compare the unscaled version, softmax(S): [[0.328, 0.308, 0.364], …]: slightly peakier, because the scores were twice as spread.

In your code

scaled_dot_product_attention: attention_weights = Softmax()(scores, dim=-1). The autograd module wraps Softmax.forward at import (tracked_softmax_forward), so the weights carry a _grad_fn and the gradient reaches Wq and Wk.

Check yourself

  • If every score in a row is increased by the same constant c, what happens to the row of A? Nothing: exp(c) cancels. Only differences between scores matter.

03 · Self-attention · Output

Output: each row becomes a weighted average of the value rows

O = A V. Row i of the output is Σj Aij vj: the values of all tokens, blended with token i's weights. This is the moment rows finally learn about each other.

O[2][0], by hand

0.3185 · 0.2447 = 0.0779
0.3201 · 0.1053 = 0.0337
0.3614 · 0.3161 = 0.1142
sum = 0.2259

A convex combination

Weights are non-negative and sum to 1, so every output row lies inside the triangle spanned by v0, v1, v2. Attention moves information; it cannot invent values that no token offered.

Unlike a Linear layer, the mixing matrix depends on the input

A Linear layer mixes features with a fixed W. Attention mixes positions with A, which is recomputed from the data for every input. That is what makes the output of row i depend on the other rows.

output = attention_weights.matmul(V) in scaled_dot_product_attention. Because A is nearly uniform at init, the three output rows are nearly identical: all three are close to the mean of V, [0.222, 0.174, −0.072, 0.177].

Visually

  • Step 1: A (3 × 3) times V (3 × 4). Step 2: O (3 × 4); the highlighted entry O[2][0] with its three products. Hover a row of O to see which rows of V it was blended from and with which weights.
  • Step 3: the two properties: convexity and input-dependence.

Mathematically

O = A V, (T × T)(T × d) → (T × d). Row i: oi = Σj Aij vj. Backward: ∂L/∂V = Aᵀ ∂L/∂O (each value row collects gradient from every row that used it, weighted) and ∂L/∂A = ∂L/∂O Vᵀ, which then flows through the softmax to S and on to Q and K.

Numerically

O = [[0.225, 0.180, −0.087, 0.184], [0.223, 0.179, −0.082, 0.181], [0.226, 0.187, −0.100, 0.188]]. The rows are almost the same because the weights are almost uniform; the differences, of order 0.01, are the only place where "who attends to whom" shows up at init. Training amplifies exactly these differences.

In your code

Tensor.matmul uses np.matmul for 3-D and 4-D operands, so one call handles the batch and head axes. The 2-D path with explicit Python loops is only hit by 2-D inputs.

Check yourself

  • Attention weights A are (T × T). Which tensor has to be the same size for A V to be defined, and which axis of it? V must have T rows: the key/value positions; its column count dv is free.

03 · Self-attention · Causal mask

The causal mask: a position may read the past, never the future

A language model predicts token t+1 from tokens ≤ t. If row t could attend to row t+1 during training it would read the answer off the input. So the upper triangle of the score table is set to −10⁹ before the softmax, which makes those weights exactly 0.

Mask arithmetic

mask = tril(ones(T, T))   1 = allowed
scores += (1 − mask) · (−1e9)
softmax([0.5, 1.2, −0.3, 0.8] masked to 2)
= [0.3318, 0.6682, 0, 0]

Row 0 can only see itself

Its weight on itself is 1 whatever the scores are: the first token's output is just v0. Row 1 splits between 0 and 1; only the last row uses the whole table.

Why −10⁹ and not 0

A weight of 0 after softmax needs a score of −∞ before it. Adding a huge negative number does that without producing NaNs, and keeps the operation a plain addition that autograd already knows how to differentiate (the masked entries get zero gradient through the softmax).

_apply_mask(scores, mask) in src/core/attention.py adds (ones − mask) · MASK_VALUE with MASK_VALUE = −1e9. create_causal_mask(T) in src/core/transformers.py returns np.tril(ones) with a leading batch axis; GPT._create_causal_mask returns the same without it (NumPy broadcasts both).

Visually

  • Step 1: the mask for T = 3: ones on and below the diagonal. Step 2: the scaled scores with −10⁹ written into the upper triangle. Step 3: softmax: the masked cells become 0.000 and each row renormalises over what is left. Step 4: the output Ocausal; row 0 equals v0 exactly.

Mathematically

S' = S/√d + (1 − M)·(−10⁹), with Mij = 1 if j ≤ i else 0. exp(−10⁹ − max) underflows to 0 in float32 and float64, so Aij = 0 for j > i and the remaining entries are the softmax over j ≤ i. The mask is a constant: no parameters, no gradient.

Numerically

Acausal = [[1, 0, 0], [0.4986, 0.5014, 0], [0.3185, 0.3201, 0.3614]]: the last row is unchanged from the unmasked A because it was allowed to see everything anyway. Ocausal[0] = [0.2447, −0.1353, 0.2263, 0.0822] = V[0]. Ocausal[1] = 0.4986·v0 + 0.5014·v1 = [0.1748, 0.0241, 0.2586, 0.0394].

In your code

MultiHeadAttention.forward reshapes a 3-D mask (B, T, T) to (B, 1, T, T) so one mask broadcasts over all heads. The 2-D mask that GPT._create_causal_mask produces skips that branch and still broadcasts against (B, h, T, T). The module-level create_causal_mask is the one to call from your own code.

Check yourself

  • At generation time, after the model has produced its answer token by token, is the mask still needed? Not for correctness of the last position, but the code applies it anyway so that the cached earlier positions stay identical to training.

03 · Self-attention · The function

scaled_dot_product_attention: five lines, two outputs, no parameters

def scaled_dot_product_attention(Q, K, V, mask=None):
    scores = Q.matmul(K.transpose(-2, -1))      # (…, T, T)
    scores = scores * (1 / sqrt(Q.shape[-1]))   # ÷ √d_k
    if mask is not None:
        scores = scores + (1 - mask) * -1e9      # future → −∞
    weights = Softmax()(scores, dim=-1)          # rows sum to 1
    return weights.matmul(V), weights            # (…, T, d_v), (…, T, T)
0
parameters inside
2T²d
multiply-adds · QKᵀ and AV
T²
weights stored per head per layer
5
backward nodes · matmul, mul, add, softmax, matmul

src/core/attention.py. The "…" in the shapes is any number of leading axes: (B,) for single-head use, (B, h) once MultiHeadAttention has split the heads. The weights are returned so a caller can inspect or plot them; MultiHeadAttention discards them.

Visually

  • Step 1: the function, condensed to its arithmetic (the real file splits it into _compute_attention_scores, _scale_scores, _apply_mask and the softmax call). Step 2: the shape flow on the right: three (…, T, d) inputs become a (…, T, T) table, which becomes a (…, T, d) output. Step 3: the costs.

Mathematically

Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QKᵀ/√dk + mask) V. The two matmuls each cost T·T·d multiply-adds; the softmax and mask are T². Memory is dominated by the (T × T) weights, which must be kept for backward. With T = 1024 and dk = 64, one head does 134M multiply-adds and stores 1M weights.

Numerically

For the "cat ate the" example (T = 3, d = 4): 9 scores, 9 weights, 72 multiply-adds. Everything in the function is determined by Q, K, V; change Wq and the whole table changes, but the function itself has nothing to train.

In your code

Each line creates a tracked Tensor: MatmulBackward, MulBackward, AddBackward, SoftmaxBackward, MatmulBackward. Tensor.backward walks them in reverse; the gradient reaches Q, K and V and from there the projection weights. The docstring example with (2, 4, 64) inputs is the single-head use; MultiHeadAttention is the 4-D use.

Check yourself

  • Which line makes the output of row t depend on the other rows, and which line makes that dependence input-dependent? The last matmul mixes rows; the first matmul plus softmax computes the mixing weights from the rows themselves.

04 · Multi-head attention · Why

One softmax row is one pattern: a single head has to choose

Row i gets one distribution over sources. If the next token depends on both the previous word and the subject further back, one row must split its mass and blur both. The fix: several distributions per row, called heads.

Two questions, one answer slot

"What came just before me?" and "who is the subject of this sentence?" want different sources. One row of weights cannot put 0.9 on both; the best it can do is 0.45 each, and the output is a blend of two unrelated values.

h heads: h rows of weights per position, side by side

Each head has its own Wq, Wk, Wv slice, its own (T × T) table and its own softmax, so it can commit fully to one pattern. The outputs are concatenated and mixed by one more Linear.

Your trained model does exactly this

Last position of "the bone . the cat sat on the", block 1: head 0 puts 0.84 on "cat" (the subject, 3 back); head 1 puts 0.76 on "on" (the previous word). Same input row, two sources, read at once.

Top: illustrative weights. Bottom: real attention rows of the trained tiny GPT (section 06), block 1 (index 0), heads 0 and 1, query = last position, probe "the bone . the cat sat on the". Values below 0.04 not labelled.

Visually

  • Step 1: the dilemma, drawn on the sentence from section 02: the row for "it" would like to read "cat" (subject) and "was" (previous token). One arc set has to carry both.
  • Step 2: two heads: each arc set belongs to one head and can be sharp. The two results sit side by side in the output row, in different columns.
  • Step 3: real rows from your trained model. The bars are attention weights of the last query position over the 8 words of the probe, for the two heads of the first block. Head 0 is a "find the subject" pattern; head 1 is a "previous word" pattern.

Mathematically

A single head produces oi = Σj aij vj with one ai·. Multi-head produces oi = Wo [Σj a(1)ij v(1)j ; … ; Σj a(h)ij v(h)j], with h independent weight rows a(k)i·. The representational gain is in the h different softmaxes, not in extra parameters.

Numerically

Block 1, head 0, last row: 0.839 on position 4 ("cat"), 0.098 on position 2 ("."). Head 1, last row: 0.760 on position 6 ("on"), 0.089 on "sat". In block 2, head 0 puts 0.95 on "sat" and head 1 another 0.84 on "cat". For the dog probe, block 1 head 0 puts 0.75 on "dog" and head 1 splits 0.49 / 0.44 between "on" and "dog": the heads divide the work differently per input.

In your code

MultiHeadAttention(embed_dim, num_heads) asserts embed_dim % num_heads == 0 and sets head_dim = embed_dim // num_heads. Everything else about heads is a reshape (next slide).

Check yourself

  • Could one head with twice the dimension replace two heads? No: it would still have a single softmax row per position, so a single pattern; the extra dimensions only make the single score more expressive.

04 · Multi-head attention · Split

Splitting d into h heads is a reshape and a transpose, not new weights

Q is still X Wq, (T × d). Head i simply takes columns i·dh … (i+1)·dh − 1. The code reshapes (B, T, d) → (B, T, h, dh) and swaps the middle axes so that each head is a separate (T × dh) matrix for the batched matmul.

def _split_heads(x, B, T):          # (B, T, d)
    x = x.reshape(B, T, h, d // h)   # (B, T, h, d_h)
    return x.transpose(1, 2)         # (B, h, T, d_h)

Each head scores with its own √dh

Head 0 of the example: q0 · k2 = 0.1062·1.2283 + (−0.0204)(0.2607) = 0.1252, divided by √2 → 0.0885. Only two products now, where the single head had four.

Same parameters, same cost, more patterns

Four Linear(d, d) layers: 4(d² + d) = 80 numbers for d = 4, whether h is 1, 2 or 4. The work is also the same: h tables of T² · (d/h) = T² d. Heads are free.

MultiHeadAttention(4, 2): head_dim = 2. Q_h0 = Q[:, 0:2], Q_h1 = Q[:, 2:4]; likewise K and V. Head scores shown are already divided by √2.

Visually

  • Step 1: Q with its four columns coloured in two pairs: head 0 (blue) gets columns 0–1, head 1 (purple) gets columns 2–3. Step 2: after reshape and transpose the same numbers are laid out as two (3 × 2) matrices; K and V are split the same way.
  • Step 3: each head computes its own (3 × 3) table of scaled scores from its own two columns. Step 4: the accounting.

Mathematically

Writing Wq = [Wq(0) | Wq(1)] by column blocks, Q(i) = X Wq(i): splitting the output columns of one Linear is the same as having h smaller Linears. S(i) = Q(i) K(i)ᵀ / √dh. The reshape is a view, not a copy; the transpose makes the head axis a batch axis so that np.matmul runs all heads at once.

Numerically

Qh0 = [[0.106, −0.020], [0.061, −0.142], [0.031, 0.170]]; Qh1 = [[−0.064, 0.091], [−0.156, 0.369], [0.204, 0.059]]. Scaled scores head 0: [[0.008, −0.040, 0.089], [−0.004, −0.027, 0.027], [0.014, −0.007, 0.058]]; head 1: [[−0.011, −0.006, −0.017], [−0.009, 0.022, 0.025], [0.073, 0.101, 0.208]]. Head 1 is where the "the" token's self-preference lives.

In your code

_split_heads and _merge_heads in src/core/attention.py; Tensor.reshape and Tensor.transpose(dim0, dim1) are tracked (ReshapeBackward, TransposeBackward), so gradients flow back through the view.

Check yourself

  • Why transpose to (B, h, T, dh) rather than keep (B, T, h, dh)? matmul contracts the last two axes; the per-head (T × dh) matrices must be the last two, with B and h in front as batch axes.

04 · Multi-head attention · Run and merge

Two heads, two tables, two half-outputs, one concatenation, one mix

Each head runs the five lines of section 03 on its slice, under the same causal mask. The two (T × dh) outputs are put side by side into a (T × d) matrix, and Wo lets the heads talk to each other.

out[0][0], by hand

concat[0] = [0.2447, −0.1353 | 0.2263, 0.0822]
· Wo[:, 0] = [−0.3207, 0.0373, −0.0333, 0.1016]
= −0.0785 − 0.0050 − 0.0075 + 0.0084 = −0.0827

Why the output projection

Without Wo, head 0 could only ever write to columns 0–1 and head 1 to columns 2–3. Wo mixes the heads' findings into every dimension, and it is the only place a head's result meets another's.

Shapes, start to end

(1, 3, 4) → q, k, v (1, 3, 4) → split (1, 2, 3, 2) → tables (1, 2, 3, 3) → attended (1, 2, 3, 2) → merge (1, 3, 4) → out_proj (1, 3, 4). Input shape in, input shape out: this is what lets the block add it back to X.

MultiHeadAttention(4, 2).forward(X, mask=create_causal_mask(3)); the figure's numbers equal the module's output to 1e−16. Row 0 of each head's output equals that head's v₀ because row 0 may only see itself.

Visually

  • Step 1: the two causal weight tables Ah0 and Ah1. They differ (0.5056/0.4944 against 0.4923/0.5077 in row 1) because the heads scored with different columns.
  • Step 2: each table times its own V slice gives a (3 × 2) output; _merge_heads transposes back to (B, T, h, dh) and reshapes to (B, T, d): head 0's two columns then head 1's two columns.
  • Step 3: the concatenation times Wo (plus a zero bias) is the layer's output, (3 × 4).

Mathematically

MultiHead(X) = Concat(head1, …, headh) Wo, headi = Attention(X Wq(i), X Wk(i), X Wv(i)). Concat followed by Wo equals Σi headi Wo(i) with Wo cut into row blocks: each head's output is projected by its own (dh × d) block and the projections are summed.

Numerically

Oh0 = [[0.2447, −0.1353], [0.1758, 0.0219], [0.2242, 0.1786]], Oh1 = [[0.2263, 0.0822], [0.2590, 0.0389], [−0.0987, 0.1877]]. concat row 1 = [0.1758, 0.0219, 0.2590, 0.0389]. Output = [[−0.0827, 0.2622, 0.2741, −0.3182], [−0.0602, 0.2595, 0.2537, −0.2085], [−0.0429, 0.1993, 0.0095, −0.1515]].

In your code

forward steps 4–6: scaled_dot_product_attention(Q, K, V, mask=mask_reshaped), _merge_heads, out_proj.forward. The returned weights are dropped (attended, _ = …); to plot them, as section 06 does, wrap the function.

Check yourself

  • GPT-2 small has d = 768 and 12 heads. What is the shape of the attention tables for a batch of 1 and T = 1024, and how many numbers is that? (1, 12, 1024, 1024): 12.6M per layer.

04 · Multi-head attention · The module

MultiHeadAttention.forward: six steps, eight parameter tensors, shape in = shape out

def forward(self, x, mask=None):               # x: (B, T, d)
    B, T, d = x.shape                            # 1. shapes
    Q, K, V = q_proj(x), k_proj(x), v_proj(x)   # 2. (B, T, d) ×3
    Q, K, V = split(Q), split(K), split(V)      # 3. (B, h, T, d_h)
    if mask is not None and mask.ndim == 3:
        mask = mask.reshape(B, 1, T, T)          # 4. one mask, all heads
    att, _ = scaled_dot_product_attention(Q, K, V, mask)
    out = merge(att)                             # 5. (B, T, d)
    return out_proj(out)                         # 6. (B, T, d)

Why not "normal" single-head self-attention?

Same parameters, same FLOPs, same shapes. The only difference is h softmax rows per position instead of one, and that difference is what lets one layer track several relations at once. There is no reason to prefer h = 1; GPT-2 uses 12, large models 32–128.

80
params · d = 4 · 4(d² + d)
2.36M
params · GPT-2 · d = 768
64
head_dim · GPT-2 · 768 / 12

parameters() returns [W_q, b_q, W_k, b_k, W_v, b_v, W_o, b_o]: four (d × d) matrices and four (d,) biases. GPT-2: 4 · (768² + 768) = 2,362,368 per block, 28.3M over 12 blocks.

Visually

  • Step 1: the method, condensed. Step 2: the eight parameter tensors as blocks, with the counts. Step 3: the answer to "why multi-head rather than plain self-attention".

Mathematically

Parameters: 4d² + 4d. FLOPs per layer (forward, one sequence): projections 4 · T d² ; tables and mixing 2 · T² d. For T < d the projections dominate; for T > d the T² term does. GPT-2 (d = 768, T = 1024): 2.4 GFLOP for projections, 1.6 GFLOP for attention proper, per layer.

Numerically

d = 4: 4 · 16 + 4 · 4 = 80. d = 768: 2,359,296 + 3,072 = 2,362,368. d = 16 (the trained tiny model): 1,088 per block.

In your code

The mask reshape in step 4 only triggers for 3-D masks. __call__ forwards to forward, so mha(x, mask) works. The weights are created by Linear with requires_grad unset (False), which is one of the fixes listed on the recap slide.

Check yourself

  • Which of the six steps would change for cross-attention over a memory of length Tm? Step 2 (K, V from the memory) and the mask shape (B, 1, T, Tm); everything else is unchanged.

05 · Transformer block · The goal

The goal: predict the next token at every position

Shift the input by one and you have the targets: row t must put probability on token t+1. Cross-entropy over all T positions, averaged, is the loss; the causal mask keeps each of those predictions honest.

Inputs and targets are the same text

x = tokens[0 … T−1], y = tokens[1 … T]. "cat ate the" + its next word gives three training examples: cat → ate, cat ate → the, cat ate the → next. One forward pass scores all of them.

The loss you already built

Logits (B, T, V) are reshaped to (B·T, V) and CrossEntropyLoss from the foundation deck does the rest: −mean log p(yt). Chance level is ln V: 2.48 nats for V = 12.

What a falling loss means here

Your tiny GPT: 3.07 → 0.32 after 50 Adam steps → about 0.25 from step 100 on. The floor is the text's own randomness: after "." either animal may follow, and after "the cat" it may sit or eat. Where the next word is determined, the model is nearly certain.

Training run: word vocabulary (V = 12) on "the dog ate the bone . the cat sat on the mat . …" (16 sentences, 107 words); GPT(V, 16, 2 layers, 2 heads, T = 8); random 8-word windows, batch 16; Adam lr 0.01; 401 steps, 2.5 s; loss through your CrossEntropyLoss and Tensor.backward.

Visually

  • Step 1: the shift. The input row and the target row are the same words, offset by one. Each position t of the logits is compared with yt = xt+1.
  • Step 2: the loss is one number per position, averaged over positions and batch. The mask guarantees position t used only x0…t, otherwise the comparison would be cheating.
  • Step 3: the real loss curve of the model trained at the end of this deck, 401 steps, with the chance line ln 12.

Mathematically

L = −(1/BT) Σb,t log softmax(logitsb,t)[yb,t]. Minimising L is maximising the likelihood of the text under the model's chain rule p(x1…T) = Πt p(xt | x<t); each factor is one row of the logits. Without the mask, p(xt | x<t) would be replaced by p(xt | everything), which is trivially 1.

Numerically

Step 0: 3.071 (above chance because the untrained logits are not flat). Step 50: 0.320. Step 100: 0.241. Step 200: 0.283. Step 400: 0.247; mean of the last 20 steps 0.254. With B = 16 and T = 8 each step averages 128 predictions. The 0.25 floor is irreducible: of the 107 words, roughly one in four is a genuine coin flip (which animal, sat or ate).

In your code

logits.reshape(B*T, V) is a tracked reshape; CrossEntropyLoss.forward is wrapped by autograd (tracked_ce_forward) and attaches CrossEntropyBackward. The training loop is the foundation one: zero_grad, backward, step. Nothing in training.py had to change.

Check yourself

  • Why does the loss start above ln V rather than at it? Random logits are not uniform; the expected cross-entropy of a random distribution is higher than that of the uniform one.

05 · Transformer block · Why a block

What attention alone cannot do, and what the block adds

What attention alone does

Output row = weighted average of value rows, then one Linear. Everything is linear in V, and V is linear in X: attention can fetch, blend and route, but not compute a non-linear function of what it fetched.

Gap 1 → MLP: compute per position

A two-layer network with GELU, applied to each row separately. Attention decides which rows to read; the MLP decides what to make of the result.

Gap 2 → residuals: edit, do not replace

One layer is one hop; multi-step reasoning needs several. Deep stacks train only if each layer adds to a shared stream, y = x + f(x), so gradients and the embedding reach every layer intact.

Gap 3 → LayerNorm: fix the scale

Sums of many layers drift in magnitude, and dot products and GELU care about scale. Normalising each row before it is read keeps every sub-layer's input in range at any depth.

The block: shape in = shape out, so stack N of them

x → LN → MHA → + x → LN → MLP → + → y, all (B, T, d). GPT-2 small stacks 12, GPT-3 96.

TransformerBlock.forward in src/core/transformers.py: normed1 = ln1(x); x = x + attention(normed1, mask); normed2 = ln2(x); output = x + mlp(normed2). Pre-norm placement, as in GPT-2.

Visually

  • Step 1: a bare attention layer between x and y. Step 2: an MLP is appended. Step 3: both sub-layers are wrapped in residual additions; the vertical line is the residual stream. Step 4: LayerNorms are placed on the branches, before each sub-layer reads the stream. Step 5: the finished block, repeated N times.

Mathematically

Attention: oi = Wo Σj aij Wv xj. For fixed weights a this is linear in X; the only non-linearity is inside a itself (the softmax), which chooses the mixture but not the content. MLP: m(x) = W2 GELU(W1 x + b1) + b2, a universal approximator per row. Residual: y = x + f(LN(x)) gives ∂y/∂x = I + ∂f/∂x·∂LN/∂x: the identity keeps gradient magnitude ≈ 1 through any number of blocks.

Numerically

In the block run (three slides on), attention adds rows of norm 2.37, 1.53, 1.09 to X rows of norm 0.47, 0.99, 1.27; the MLP adds 1.08, 0.79, 1.89 more. Without normalisation the next block would see inputs 2–3× larger than this one did; LayerNorm resets them to norm √d = 2 exactly (γ = 1, β = 0).

In your code

TransformerBlock.__init__ owns attention, ln1, ln2, mlp; forward(x, mask) is the four lines quoted under the figure. The dropout argument is accepted and unused.

Check yourself

  • Which of the three additions is essential for training depth, which for expressiveness, which for stability? Residuals: depth. MLP: expressiveness. LayerNorm: stability.

05 · Transformer block · LayerNorm

LayerNorm: put every row on the same scale before it is read

For each row, subtract its mean and divide by its standard deviation over the d features, then let two learned vectors γ and β rescale and shift. Rows are normalised independently: no batch statistics, no dependence on T.

Row 0, by hand

μ = mean(−0.196, −0.029, −0.353, 0.247) = −0.0828
σ² = 0.0493   σ = √(σ² + 10⁻⁵) = 0.2222
(−0.196 − (−0.0828)) / 0.2222 = −0.5114

γ and β: 2d parameters

Start at ones and zeros, so LN is a pure standardisation at init. Training can undo the normalisation for features that should keep a scale, or shift the mean. Every normalised row has norm √d = 2 here.

Pre-norm vs post-norm

GPT-2 and this code normalise the input of each sub-layer and leave the residual stream untouched. The original Transformer normalised after the addition. Pre-norm trains more stably at depth; it needs the extra ln_f before the head.

LayerNorm(4) on X; eps = 1e−5. Means [−0.083, −0.040, −0.413], variances [0.049, 0.246, 0.232]. Backward: _LayerNormBackward implements dx = (γ/σ)(g − mean(g) − x̂ · mean(g · x̂)) in one Function.

Visually

  • Step 1: the three rows of X as bars: different means, different spreads. Step 2: each row's μ and σ, then (x − μ)/σ: every row now centred at 0 with unit variance. Step 3: γ ⊙ x̂ + β with γ = 1, β = 0 leaves it unchanged at init.

Mathematically

x̂ = (x − μ)/√(σ² + ε), y = γ ⊙ x̂ + β, with μ, σ² over the last axis. Backward (per row): ∂L/∂β = Σ g, ∂L/∂γ = Σ g ⊙ x̂, ∂L/∂x = (1/σ) [g ⊙ γ − mean(g ⊙ γ) − x̂ · mean(g ⊙ γ ⊙ x̂)]. The two subtracted terms are the gradients through μ and σ. Compare BatchNorm, which uses statistics across the batch and behaves differently at train and test time; LayerNorm is the same in both.

Numerically

LN(X) = [[−0.511, 0.244, −1.216, 1.483], [−0.176, 1.288, −1.476, 0.364], [−1.365, −0.222, 1.437, 0.151]]. Each row has mean 0 and Σx̂² = 4 − 4·10⁻⁵/σ² ≈ 4, so norm ≈ 2. Note how row 0, the smallest row of X (norm 0.47), is stretched the most (÷0.22) and row 1 the least (÷0.50).

In your code

LayerNorm.forward computes with NumPy and attaches _LayerNormBackward(x, gamma, beta, normalized, std) itself rather than composing tracked ops: one node instead of seven, and the formula above in apply. gamma and beta are created with requires_grad=True, the only parameters in the stack that are.

Check yourself

  • Why is ε inside the square root? A row of identical values has σ² = 0; ε keeps the division finite and the gradient bounded.

05 · Transformer block · MLP

MLP: widen each row, bend it with GELU, bring it back

Linear(d, 4d) → GELU → Linear(4d, d), applied to every position on its own: the foundation MLP with a smoother activation and no interaction between rows. Attention communicates; this computes.

GELU, as implemented

GELU(x) = x · σ(1.702 x)  ≈  x · Φ(x)
x = 0.866 → 0.704 (exact 0.698)
x = −1.876 → −0.074 (exact −0.057)

Negative inputs are damped, not cut to zero as ReLU would: the curve is smooth, and a small negative gradient survives.

Two thirds of the block's parameters

8d² + 5d: 148 of the block's 244 for d = 4; 4.72M of 7.09M for GPT-2. The 4× width is a convention from the original Transformer; the hidden layer is where facts are thought to be stored.

Per position = batched over positions

The (B, T, d) tensor is treated as B·T independent rows: same weights, no mixing. The same code path as Linear on a batch of vectors in the foundation deck.

MLP(4): linear1 = Linear(4, 16), gelu = GELU(), linear2 = Linear(16, 4). Row shown: LN(X)[0]. GELU in src/core/activations.py uses the sigmoid approximation x · σ(1.702x); exact values from x · Φ(x) for comparison.

Visually

  • Step 1: row 0 of LN(X), four numbers, goes through Linear(4, 16): sixteen pre-activations (bars). Step 2: GELU bends them: large positives pass, negatives shrink towards zero; the curve on the right is x · σ(1.702x) with the exact x · Φ(x) as dots. Step 3: Linear(16, 4) returns to four numbers: the same shape as the row that went in, ready to be added back to the stream.

Mathematically

m(x) = W2 GELU(x W1 + b1) + b2, W1: (d × 4d), W2: (4d × d). GELU(x) = x Φ(x) where Φ is the standard normal CDF; the code uses σ(1.702x) ≈ Φ(x), accurate to about 0.02. Parameters: d·4d + 4d + 4d·d + d = 8d² + 5d.

Numerically

Pre-activations for row 0: [0.114, −0.256, 0.866, 0.148, 0.692, −0.022, 0.454, −0.766, 0.833, 0.046, −0.537, −1.876, −0.690, 0.617, −1.942, −0.007]. After GELU: [0.063, −0.101, 0.704, 0.083, 0.529, −0.011, 0.311, −0.164, 0.670, 0.024, −0.154, −0.074, −0.163, 0.457, −0.069, −0.003]. Output row 0: [−0.361, −0.129, 0.313, −0.507]. Table of the approximation: x = −3 → −0.018 (exact −0.004); −1 → −0.154 (−0.159); 1 → 0.846 (0.841); 3 → 2.982 (2.996).

In your code

MLP.forward: linear1 → gelu → linear2. GELU.forward is Sigmoid()(x * 1.702) * x, composed from tracked ops, so its backward is assembled by autograd from SigmoidBackward and two MulBackwards. hidden_dim defaults to 4·embed_dim; TransformerBlock passes mlp_ratio or ff_dim.

Check yourself

  • Why can the MLP not fix the "cat ate the" / "wolf ate the" gap of the recap on its own? It is row-wise: identical rows in give identical rows out. Only attention changes a row based on other rows.

05 · Transformer block · Residuals

Residual connections: edit the stream, do not replace it

y = x + f(LN(x)). The stream that enters the block leaves it with two additions. Forward, the embedding is still present at the top of a 12-block stack; backward, ∂y/∂x = I + … hands the gradient straight through.

Row norms along the stream

X: 0.47 · 0.99 · 1.27
+ attention (2.37 · 1.53 · 1.09)
x₁: 2.07 · 1.68 · 1.79
+ MLP (1.08 · 0.79 · 1.89)
y: 2.75 · 2.05 · 3.43

The gradient highway

∂L/∂x = ∂L/∂y · (I + ∂f/∂x). Even if a sub-layer's Jacobian is tiny, the identity term delivers the full gradient to the block below. Twelve blocks deep, the embedding table still gets a direct signal.

Why the head can be tied to the embedding

Because the stream is additive, the final representation is "embedding + corrections". Reading it out with the embedding matrix transposed (GPT-2's tied lm_head) is natural; this code keeps a separate Linear(d, V).

TransformerBlock(4, 2) on X with the causal mask; norms are Euclidean norms of the three rows at each point of the stream. The attention branch here reads LN(X), so its weights differ from the MHA-on-X numbers of sections 03–04.

Visually

  • Step 1: the stream as a horizontal bar from X to y, with the two branches (attention, MLP) tapping it and writing back through ⊕. Step 2: the row norms at each point as bars; the stream grows because each branch adds. Step 3: the backward arrows: gradient flows along the bar unchanged and additionally through each branch.

Mathematically

y = x + g(x), g = f ∘ LN. Chain rule: ∂L/∂x = ∂L/∂y + ∂L/∂y · ∂g/∂x. Across N blocks the Jacobian is Π (I + Ji), which contains the identity plus all products of subsets of Ji: a sum of paths of every length, the short ones carrying gradient even when long ones vanish. Autograd implements this without special code: AddBackward passes the gradient to both inputs.

Numerically

x₁ = X + attention(LN(X)): row 0 = [−0.196, −0.029, −0.353, 0.247] + [−0.424, 1.228, 1.297, −1.500] = [−0.620, 1.200, 0.944, −1.253]. y = x₁ + MLP(LN(x₁)): row 0 = [−0.620, 1.200, 0.944, −1.253] + [−0.696, −0.357, 0.651, −0.351] = [−1.316, 0.843, 1.595, −1.605]. The branches are 2–5× larger than X at init; in training, the output projections learn to write with appropriate size.

In your code

Two lines: x = x + attention_out and output = x + mlp_out. In Tensor.backward the recursion visits x twice (once per path), which is correct because gradients accumulate with +=; it also means the sub-graph below each fork is traversed once per path, so cost grows exponentially with depth, something to fix before training deep models.

Check yourself

  • What would happen to the norms above after 12 blocks if there were no LayerNorm? Each block adds terms proportional to its input scale; magnitudes would compound block after block.

05 · Transformer block · The run

TransformerBlock on X: seven tensors from input to output

def forward(self, x, mask=None):
    normed1 = self.ln1(x)
    x = x + self.attention(normed1, mask)
    normed2 = self.ln2(x)
    return x + self.mlp(normed2)

244 parameters for d = 4

attention 4d² + 4d = 80 · ln1, ln2 2d each = 16 · MLP 8d² + 5d = 148. Total 12d² + 13d. The same block at d = 768: 7,087,872, of which the MLP is 4.72M and attention 2.36M.

Shape in = shape out, mask passed through

(1, 3, 4) → (1, 3, 4). The block does not know where it sits in the stack; GPT calls it in a loop with the same mask, and each block has its own 244 numbers.

TransformerBlock(embed_dim=4, num_heads=2).forward(X, create_causal_mask(3)), fresh process: its attention is the first module constructed, so its W_q, W_k, W_v, W_o are the matrices of sections 03–04; ln1, ln2 start at γ = 1, β = 0; MLP weights are the next draws.

Visually

  • Steps 1–6: the seven (3 × 4) tensors appear left to right: X, LN₁(X), attention output, x₁ = X + attention, LN₂(x₁), MLP output, y = x₁ + MLP. Tinted frames mark the two normalisations (teal), the attention branch (amber), the MLP branch (brown) and the stream (ink).
  • Step 7: the parameter accounting and the shape invariant.

Mathematically

n₁ = LN₁(X); a = MHA(n₁; mask); x₁ = X + a; n₂ = LN₂(x₁); m = MLP(n₂); y = x₁ + m. Six operations, two of which (the additions) have no parameters and the other four carry 80 + 8 + 8 + 148 numbers.

Numerically

n₁ = LN(X) from the LayerNorm slide. a = [[−0.424, 1.228, 1.297, −1.500], [−0.256, 0.877, 0.882, −0.850], [−0.208, 0.713, 0.472, −0.638]]. x₁ = [[−0.620, 1.200, 0.944, −1.253], [−0.383, 1.475, 0.111, −0.709], [−1.278, 0.193, 0.751, −0.979]]. n₂ = [[−0.666, 1.096, 0.849, −1.279], [−0.608, 1.622, −0.015, −0.999], [−1.143, 0.628, 1.299, −0.783]]. m = [[−0.696, −0.357, 0.651, −0.351], [−0.590, −0.141, 0.165, −0.477], [−0.923, −0.678, 1.451, −0.378]]. y = [[−1.316, 0.843, 1.595, −1.605], [−0.973, 1.334, 0.275, −1.186], [−2.201, −0.484, 2.203, −1.357]].

In your code

TransformerBlock.parameters() concatenates attention (8 tensors), ln1 (2), ln2 (2), mlp (4): 16 tensors, 244 numbers. The block's own forward is the five lines shown; the dropout_prob argument is unused.

Check yourself

  • Which two of the seven tensors would change if you swapped the order of the attention and MLP sub-layers? All of them from the second onwards; only X is independent of the block's internals.

06 · GPT · Architecture

GPT: the embedding you built, N blocks, a final norm, a head

Similar: every part is a module you already have

EmbeddingLayer from deck 01; TransformerBlock from section 05, repeated; LayerNorm once more; Linear(d, V, bias=False) from the foundation deck; Softmax and CrossEntropyLoss to read and train it.

Different: the same block, N different sets of weights

Blocks share the architecture, not the parameters: for _ in range(num_layers): TransformerBlock(…). Each sees the same (B, T, T) mask. Depth is what turns one hop into a chain of hops.

Different: a head over the vocabulary, no bias

lm_head maps each row from d to V: one score per vocabulary entry per position. It is the embedding table in the other direction (V × d against d × V); GPT-2 literally reuses the same matrix.

GPT(vocab_size=6, embed_dim=4, num_layers=2, num_heads=2, max_seq_len=8) on ids [[2, 1, 3]], fresh process (with the Embeddinglayer typo patched to run). Logits (1, 3, 6); probabilities are softmax over the last axis.

Visually

  • Step 1: tokens (1, 3) enter the EmbeddingLayer and come out as X (1, 3, 4). Step 2: two blocks, each (1, 3, 4) → (1, 3, 4), with the mask drawn once and fed to both. Step 3: ln_f normalises the final stream. Step 4: lm_head gives logits (1, 3, 6): one row per position, one column per vocabulary entry, shown with the softmaxed probabilities beside them.

Mathematically

X⁰ = Emb(ids) + P[:T]; Xˡ = Blockl(Xˡ⁻¹; M) for l = 1…N; logits = LNf(Xᴺ) Whead, Whead: (d × V). p(next = v | x≤t) = softmax(logitst)v. The whole model is a function from (B, T) integers to (B, T, V) reals; the mask makes column t depend on inputs ≤ t only.

Numerically

Logits = [[0.539, −0.479, −0.771, 0.222, 1.263, −0.702], [−0.349, −1.083, −1.438, −0.346, 1.038, −0.570], [−0.073, 0.495, −1.374, 0.163, −0.302, 0.402]]. Probabilities = [[0.212, 0.077, 0.057, 0.155, 0.438, 0.061], [0.131, 0.063, 0.044, 0.132, 0.525, 0.105], [0.149, 0.263, 0.041, 0.189, 0.119, 0.240]]. Untrained, the model favours "tuna" (id 4) after "cat" and after "cat ate", and "ate" after "cat ate the". 576 parameters: 24 + 32 + 2·244 + 8 + 24.

In your code

GPT.__init__ builds embedding_layer, blocks, ln_f, lm_head; forward builds the mask with _create_causal_mask(seq_len) and loops over the blocks. The constructor currently names the class Embeddinglayer (lower-case l), which raises NameError until corrected. parameters() returns 37 tensors for this configuration.

Check yourself

  • Which rows of the logits are legitimate predictions for training, and which row would you use for generation? All T rows train (row t predicts token t+1); generation reads only the last row.

06 · GPT · Reading the output

From logits to text: softmax per position, then sample

Softmax over the vocabulary turns row t into p(next | x≤t). To write text, take the last row, sample a token, append it and run again; temperature divides the logits first (below 1 sharpens, above 1 flattens).

for _ in range(max_new_tokens):
    logits = self.forward(tokens)        # (1, T, V)
    last = logits.data[:, -1, :] / temperature
    p = softmax(last)
    nxt = rng.choice(V, p=p[0])
    tokens = concat(tokens, [[nxt]])     # T grows by 1

Context must be cropped

generate never trims tokens to max_seq_len, so the position table runs out: "Sequence length exceeds maximum: 17 > 16" after a few tokens. Feed tokens[:, −max_seq_len:] to forward.

What the trained tiny model writes

τ = 0.5: "the cat sat on the mat . the cat sat on the mat . the cat sat on the mat . the cat sat"
τ = 1.0: "the dog sat on the log . the cat ate the fish . the dog sat on the log . the dog sat on"

23 words from the prompt "the", context cropped to 8. Every sentence is grammatical and from the corpus; at τ = 0.5 sampling locks onto the likeliest sentence, at τ = 1.0 it recombines all four.

Left: softmax rows of GPT(6, 4, 2, 2, 8) on "cat ate the", untrained. Generation text: the trained model of the next slide, sampled with numpy default_rng(1), context cropped to 8 in the scratch loop (GPT.generate itself raises). _sample_next_token in src/core/transformers.py.

Visually

  • Step 1: the three probability rows of the untrained micro-model as bar charts over the six-entry vocabulary: after "cat", after "cat ate", after "cat ate the". Step 2: the generation loop. Step 3: the cropping bug. Step 4: real samples from the trained model at two temperatures.

Mathematically

pt = softmax(logitst / τ). τ → 0 is argmax (greedy); τ = 1 samples from the model's distribution; τ > 1 flattens towards uniform. Autoregressive generation computes p(xT+1 | x1…T), appends a sample, and repeats: the full forward pass is redone each step (no KV cache here), so writing n tokens costs O(n · T² d) in attention.

Numerically

Untrained rows: after "cat", p("tuna") = 0.438 is the largest; after "cat ate the", p("ate") = 0.263 and p("wolf") = 0.240. These are the random initial preferences that training replaces. The trained model after "the bone . the cat sat on the" gives "mat" 0.994, "log" 0.003 and essentially 0 to the other ten words.

In your code

GPT.generate copies the prompt, loops, takes logits.data[:, -1, :], calls _sample_next_token (temperature, stable softmax, rng.choice) and concatenates with NumPy. It runs under autograd tracking; wrapping it in no_grad() would avoid building a graph nobody uses.

Check yourself

  • Why does the loop recompute all T positions although only the last one is read? Because this implementation has no cache; K and V of earlier positions could be stored and reused, which is what a KV cache does.

06 · GPT · Trained

Trained: attention learned to look back to the subject

probeweights

Four heatmaps, one query row each

Rows are query positions, columns are the words read; the upper triangle is the mask. Hover a cell for its weight. The bottom row of each map is the last position, the one that predicts the next word.

Before and after

At init the maps are blurry and both probes get the same guess ("log", 0.42 and 0.41): the blindness of the recap, measured. After 401 steps the maps have sharp columns and the next-word bars collapse onto "mat" (0.99) or "log" (1.00).

Where the subject is found

Cat probe: block 1 head 0 puts 0.84 of the last row's weight on "cat", 3 positions back, and block 2 head 1 another 0.84. Dog probe: block 1 head 0 puts 0.75 on "dog". The information the row-wise layers could never reach is now in the last row.

Attention weights captured by wrapping scaled_dot_product_attention during the probe forward passes of the trained GPT(V=12, d=16, 2 layers, 2 heads, T=8). Loss 3.07 → 0.25 in 401 steps. Bars: softmax of the last logits row over the 12-word vocabulary.

Visually

  • Step 1: the four attention tables (2 layers × 2 heads) for the chosen probe, 8 × 8 each, dark = high weight. Below them, the model's distribution over the next word. Switch probe (cat/dog) and weights (at init/trained) with the buttons; hover cells to read exact values.
  • Step 2: what to look for: a column that lights up in the last row far to the left is the model reaching back for the subject.

Mathematically

Each map is A = softmax(QKᵀ/√8 + mask) for one head (head_dim = 16/2 = 8). The last row a7,· is the mixture that produced the last position's output in that head; the next-word distribution is softmax of the final logits row. Rows always sum to 1, so a 0.84 entry means that head's output at the last position is 84 % the value vector of one word.

Numerically

Cat, trained, last row: L1H0 → "cat" 0.84, "." 0.10; L1H1 → "on" 0.76, "sat" 0.09; L2H0 → "sat" 0.95; L2H1 → "cat" 0.84, "the" 0.05. Dog, trained: L1H0 → "dog" 0.75, "." 0.16; L1H1 → "on" 0.49, "dog" 0.44; L2H0 → "sat" 0.62, "the" 0.15; L2H1 → "dog" 0.22, "the" 0.18, "on" 0.18. Next word: cat → mat 0.994, log 0.003; dog → log 0.996, mat 0.002. Before training: cat → log 0.418, sat 0.218; dog → log 0.412, dog 0.168.

In your code

To see these maps from your own run: replace core.attention.scaled_dot_product_attention with a wrapper that stores the second return value before MultiHeadAttention.forward discards it, or make forward keep self.last_weights. Training needed four fixes listed on the recap slide; with them, 401 steps took 2.5 s on CPU.

Check yourself

  • Why is the first column of every map so often dark in the top rows but not in the bottom row? Early rows have few allowed sources, so the mass concentrates on them; the last row has eight choices.

06 · GPT · Parameters

Where the parameters live: 576 here, 124M in GPT-2 small, same five knobs

Count = V·d (tokens) + Lmax·d (positions) + N·(12d² + 13d) (blocks) + 2d (final norm) + V·d (head, unless tied). Move the sliders to see which term wins.

The micro model: 576

6·4 = 24 token rows, 8·4 = 32 position rows, 2 × 244 block parameters, 8 in ln_f, 4·6 = 24 in the head. 37 tensors from parameters().

GPT-2 small: 124,439,808

38.6M tokens (31 %), 0.79M positions, 85.1M in 12 blocks (68 %: 28.3M attention, 56.7M MLP, 37k LayerNorm), 1.5k in ln_f. The head is tied to the token table, so it adds nothing; untied it would add another 38.6M.

Blocks scale with d², tables with d

Doubling d quadruples the blocks and doubles the tables, so at scale the tables shrink to a few percent. Doubling N doubles only the blocks. V matters most for small d: at d = 16 your 12-word vocabulary (table plus untied head) is already 5 % of the model.

Counts computed from the module shapes: Linear (in × out + out), LayerNorm 2d, Embedding V × d, PositionalEncoding L × d. GPT-2 small: V = 50,257, d = 768, N = 12, L_max = 1,024, tied head. Sliders assume L_max = 1,024 and a tied head.

Visually

  • Step 1: the 576 parameters of the micro model as a bar split into tables, blocks, final norm and head. Step 2: the same bar for GPT-2 small; the blocks dominate. Step 3: sliders for d, N and V recompute the bar and the total live.

Mathematically

P(V, d, N, Lmax) = V d + Lmax d + N(12d² + 13d) + 2d (+ V d if untied). Per block: attention 4d² + 4d, two LayerNorms 4d, MLP 8d² + 5d. The d² term comes from the eight (d × d)-sized matrices per block (four in attention, the MLP's two count as four each because of the 4× width).

Numerically

Micro: 24 + 32 + 488 + 8 + 24 = 576. Tiny trained model (V = 12, d = 16, N = 2, Lmax = 8): 192 + 128 + 2·(12·256 + 208) + 32 + 192 = 7,104. GPT-2 small: 38,597,376 + 786,432 + 12·7,087,872 + 1,536 = 124,439,808.

In your code

GPT.parameters() is the concatenation of embedding_layer.parameters() (2 tensors with learned positions), each block's 16, ln_f's 2 and lm_head's 1 (no bias). Summing p.data.size over it reproduces the numbers above.

Check yourself

  • For which d does the block term equal the token table term in GPT-2's configuration (N = 12, V = 50,257)? 12·12d² ≈ 50,257 d → d ≈ 349: above that, blocks dominate.

06 · GPT · Same and different

Same and different: the new pieces against the ones you already had

PAIR
WHAT IS THE SAME
WHAT IS DIFFERENT

Reading the table

Each row pairs a component from this deck with its closest relative from the earlier decks. The left column is what carries over unchanged (so you can reuse the mental model), the right column is the one idea that is genuinely new.

Check yourself, across the deck

  • Which single property distinguishes attention from every layer in the foundation deck? Its mixing weights are computed from the input.
  • Why is the block's output the same shape as its input, and what would break otherwise? So it can be added to the stream and stacked; a shape change would make the residual addition impossible.
  • Which parts of GPT would you keep if you built an encoder (BERT-style) instead? Everything except the causal mask, and the head would predict masked tokens rather than next tokens.

07 · Recap

Recap: every piece, its shapes, its parameters, its forward and its backward

COMPONENT
IN → OUT
PARAMS
FORWARD
BACKWARD

In your code: what to fix before GPT trains end to end

transformers.py: Embeddinglayer → EmbeddingLayer in GPT.__init__; crop to tokens[:, −max_seq_len:] in generate. embeddings.py: self.indices.dota → .data; PositionalEncoding.forward wraps pos_embeddings.data[np.newaxis] in a new Tensor, which detaches P from the graph, so the position table never learns: reshape the sliced Tensor instead. layers.py, embeddings.py: create weights, biases and tables with requires_grad=True (only LayerNorm's γ, β have it today).

Next

The tiny-language-model milestone from the roadmap: overfit one batch, train on a small corpus, generate, save and reload a checkpoint with identical logits. Then the framework bridge (Module, Parameter, state_dict) so that parameters() stops being hand-written, and Tensor.backward as a topological pass so residual forks are visited once.

Check yourself, across the deck

  • In one sentence each: what do Q, K and V represent? Q: what a position is looking for. K: what a position advertises. V: what a position hands over when chosen.
  • Why √dk and why the causal mask? √dk keeps score variance at 1 so the softmax has gradient; the mask prevents reading the answer during next-token training.
  • Why heads, in one sentence? Several softmax rows per position let one layer follow several relations at once at the same parameter and compute cost.
  • Why a block rather than stacked attention? Attention only mixes linearly; the MLP computes, residuals make depth trainable, LayerNorm keeps scale.
  • What is GPT's objective, and where does the mask enter it? Mean cross-entropy of next-token predictions at all positions; the mask makes each position's prediction depend only on its past.

Numbers to remember

Attention per block: 4d² + 4d. MLP: 8d² + 5d. Block: 12d² + 13d (244 at d = 4, 7.09M at d = 768). GPT-2 small: 124.4M with tied head, 12 blocks, 12 heads of 64, context 1,024. Your tiny model: 7,104 parameters, loss 3.07 → 0.25, 2.5 s for 401 steps.
